passage:
I'm Amandeep, and I share a desk row with Chandrika, so I've seen her this month. It began on the fifteenth, when she put her name to a delivery report that she knew had one wrong figure. She said afterwards it was her manager's idea. She didn't say it was fine.

For two weeks she stopped eating lunch with us. I noticed her rereading that report at her desk more than once, jaw tight. I can't say for sure what she was thinking.

Last Wednesday, she walked into her manager's office and stayed for twenty minutes. When she came out she told me quietly, "I've corrected the record and sent the client a note." A day later the manager asked her to sign off on another report with a similar figure. She said no.

She still looks tired. But she's eating lunch with us again.

qa.q: On what date did Chandrika sign the report with the wrong figure?
qa.a: Chandrika signed it on the fifteenth.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have been feeling during the two weeks, and how sure can Amandeep be?
qa.a: Chandrika seemed troubled, shown by skipping lunch and rereading the report with a tight jaw, but Amandeep says the inner thoughts can't be known for sure.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that turned guilt into repair?
qa.a: Chandrika corrected the record, sent the client a note, and refused to sign a second report with a similar figure.

qa.q: How might the manager see Chandrika's refusal to sign the next report?
qa.a: The manager may be annoyed or uneasy, since Chandrika had gone along before and is now saying no, which changes what the manager can expect.

grounding: Chandrika went along once and feels sick about it; an observer sees her come clean, correct the record and refuse a second time.

passage:
In March, at the Valencia food lab, Santiago had asked Clara to re-run the allergen test on the granola batch until it came back clean, then log only the clean result. She had done it once. The first result showed traces of peanut.
Since then she had felt sick every time she saw that granola on supermarket shelves. She didn't eat properly for days. She kept telling herself it was only a trace.
On a Monday in May she went to the quality director's office with a printout of both results. "I logged only the clean test in March. It was wrong. The first one showed peanut traces."
The director went pale, then thanked her and ordered a recall check that afternoon.
When Santiago asked her to "be flexible" again in June, Clara said, "No. I did it once. I won't do it again."

qa.q: What did the first allergen test show?
What was Clara feeling after going along in March?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sick every time she saw the granola in shops, and couldn't eat properly for days.

qa.q: How did Clara turn her guilt into repair?
qa.a: She went to the quality director with both results, admitted what she had done, and refused when asked to do it again in June.

qa.q: How might the quality director have felt hearing Clara's admission?
qa.a: The director was shocked, going pale, but grateful that Clara came forward so a recall check could start.

grounding: The protagonist went along with falsifying a result once and feels sick; she comes clean, corrects the record and refuses a second time.

passage:
Six weeks ago at the district hospital in Nashik, Rukmini, the ward in-charge, had initialled the hand-hygiene audit form that Mohit, the infection-control officer, filled in without watching a single round. "Ninety-five per cent, as usual," he'd said. She had signed.
Since then, every time a patient on the ward ran a fever, she felt a knot in her chest. She avoided Mohit in the corridor. She told herself it didn't matter.
It did. On Thursday she went to the medical superintendent's office. "I signed an audit form last month without the audit being done. I want to correct it, and I want a real audit on my ward." The superintendent listened carefully and arranged one for the next week.
When Mohit brought the next form, already filled, Rukmini handed it back. "Not this time. I'll walk the round with you tomorrow."

qa.q: What percentage did Mohit write on the audit form?
What was Rukmini feeling after she signed the form?
qa.a: She felt guilty and anxious, with a knot in her chest whenever a patient on the ward ran a fever.

qa.q: How did Rukmini repair what she had done?
qa.a: She told the medical superintendent, asked to correct the record and have a real audit, and refused to sign the next pre-filled form.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Rukmini's refusal?
qa.a: Mohit may be surprised and uneasy, realising the shortcut is no longer accepted and he will have to do the real round.

grounding: The protagonist went along once with a falsified audit and feels sick; she comes clean, corrects the record and refuses a second time.
